title: Long-term capital gains on listed equity shares and equity-oriented fund units (STT-paid)
assetClass: Indian listed equity and equity-oriented mutual funds
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.112A read with s.2(42A). Retained in substance under the Income-tax Act, 2025 for Tax Year 2026-27 onwards (capital-gains provisions carried forward; individual section mapping pending verification).
holdingPeriodRule: More than 12 months from the date of acquisition for listed equity shares, units of equity-oriented funds and units of a business trust.
taxRate: 12.5% on gains exceeding the aggregate annual exemption, without indexation and without the currency-translation benefit.
exemptionLimit: Aggregate ₹1,25,000 per financial year across all s.112A-eligible assets. The exemption is applied once, not per transaction.
surchargeRule: Surcharge on tax under s.112A is capped at 15% regardless of total income, because the enhanced 25%/37% rates do not apply to s.111A, s.112 and s.112A income.
cessRule: Health and education cess at 4% of income tax plus surcharge.
setOffRule: Long-term capital loss on s.112A assets may be set off only against long-term capital gains and may be carried forward for up to eight assessment years if the return is filed by the due date. Note that s.112A losses can be set off against other s.112A gains, while a s.112A loss cannot be set off against gains that are not eligible for the concessional rate.
conditions: Securities transaction tax must have been paid on the transfer.
The asset must be a listed equity share, a unit of an equity-oriented fund, or a unit of a business trust.
The ₹1,25,000 exemption is available only to a resident individual or HUF for s.112A purposes.
Grandfathering of fair market value as on 31 January 2018 continues to apply to assets acquired before that date.
workedExampleSummary: Purchase ₹10,00,000; sale ₹18,00,000 after 20 months. Gain ₹8,00,000. Taxable gain after the ₹1,25,000 exemption is ₹6,75,000. Tax at 12.5% is ₹84,375; with 4% cess, ₹87,750, before any surcharge.
notes: The ₹1,25,000 exemption and the 12.5% rate took effect for transfers on or after 23 July 2024. Both are confirmed by the Income Tax Department's AY 2026-27 guidance (s.112A eligibility for ITR-1 up to ₹1,25,000) and cross-checked against secondary commentary.

title: Short-term capital gains on listed equity shares and equity-oriented fund units (STT-paid)
assetClass: Indian listed equity and equity-oriented mutual funds
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.111A. Retained in substance under the Income-tax Act, 2025 for Tax Year 2026-27 onwards.
holdingPeriodRule: 12 months or less.
taxRate: 20% flat, on the gross gain. This rate applies instead of the slab rates that would otherwise apply.
exemptionLimit: None. The s.112A ₹1,25,000 exemption does not apply to short-term gains.
surchargeRule: Surcharge capped at 15%, because the enhanced 25%/37% rates do not apply to s.111A income.
cessRule: Health and education cess at 4% of income tax plus surcharge.
setOffRule: Short-term capital losses may be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains. Losses may be carried forward for up to eight assessment years if the return is filed by the due date.
conditions: Securities transaction tax must have been paid on the transfer.
Book profits on which securities transaction tax is paid do not change the character of the gain.
A s.111A loss cannot be set off against gains on assets that are not subject to s.111A, other than long-term capital gains, in accordance with the general inter-head sequencing of s.70 and s.74.
workedExampleSummary: Purchase ₹5,00,000; sale ₹6,20,000 after 7 months. Gain ₹1,20,000. Tax at 20% is ₹24,000; with 4% cess, ₹24,960. No exemption applies.
notes: The rate moved from 15% to 20% for transfers on or after 23 July 2024. Because the rate is flat rather than slab-based, a taxpayer in the 0% slab still pays 20% on these gains.

title: Capital gains framework for Tax Year 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 2025
assessmentYear: Tax Year 2026-27 (no separate assessment year under the 2025 Act)
provision: Income-tax Act, 2025 — capital-gains provisions. The Act replaces the previous-year and assessment-year structure with a single tax year and renumbers sections (e.g. the new-regime provision formerly at s.115BAC is now s.202; the rebate formerly at s.87A is now s.156; TDS is consolidated at s.393). The individual capital-gains section numbers under the 2025 Act have not yet been independently confirmed by Arthanomy.
holdingPeriodRule: The 12-month and 24-month holding thresholds continue to apply by asset type.
taxRate: The capital-gains framework is carried forward unchanged: 20% for STT-paid short-term equity gains, 12.5% for most long-term gains with a ₹1,25,000 exemption for s.112A-type assets, and slab rates for specified mutual funds acquired on or after 1 April 2023.
exemptionLimit: ₹1,25,000 aggregate annual exemption for the s.112A-type long-term gains.
surchargeRule: Surcharge bands unchanged: nil up to ₹50 lakh, 10% to ₹1 crore, 15% to ₹2 crore, 25% to ₹5 crore, and 25% (new regime) or 37% (old regime) above ₹5 crore, with the 15% cap preserved for capital-gains and dividend income.
setOffRule: Loss set-off and eight-year carry-forward continue as before.
conditions: Arthanomy flags this rule as provisional: the substance is confirmed, the new section numbering is not yet individually verified against the Gazette text.
Once the section mapping is confirmed, this rule will be split into asset-specific entries and this consolidated entry will be marked superseded.
notes: The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026. Arthanomy expects to re-verify after the first assessment cycle under the new Act. Readers making a decision based on a specific section reference should confirm the corresponding provision in the 2025 Act via the Income Tax Department's official mapping utility.

title: Long-term capital gains on immovable property
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.112 read with s.2(42A).
holdingPeriodRule: More than 24 months. The holding period for immovable property was reduced from 36 months to 24 months with effect from 23 July 2024.
taxRate: 12.5% without indexation. For a resident individual or HUF, where the property was acquired before 23 July 2024, there is a transitional option to pay 20% with indexation instead, whichever produces the lower tax. The option is available only to resident individuals and HUFs and only for the transitional case.
exemptionLimit: Not a flat exemption. Relief is available through the s.54, s.54B, s.54D, s.54EC and s.54F routes subject to their individual conditions.
surchargeRule: Surcharge capped at 15% for s.112 income.
setOffRule: Long-term capital loss on property may be set off only against long-term capital gains. Short-term losses on property may be set off against both.
conditions: Cost of acquisition may be replaced by fair market value as on 1 April 2001 if the asset was acquired earlier.
Cost of improvement incurred before 1 April 2001 is ignored.
Transfer expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer is deductible.
s.54EC bonds: exemption up to ₹50 lakh if invested within six months in specified bonds, with a five-year lock-in on the bonds.
workedExampleSummary: Sale ₹50,00,000; cost ₹25,00,000 incurred in February 2020. Without indexation: gain ₹25,00,000, tax at 12.5% = ₹3,12,500. With indexation at 20%: indexed cost ₹31,22,923, gain ₹18,77,076, tax ₹3,75,415. The no-indexation option is better in this case. The Cost Inflation Index values used must be the notified values for the relevant financial years.
notes: The indexation comparison is highly sensitive to the acquisition year and the Cost Inflation Index. Any worked example must state the CII values used and the financial years to which they apply.

title: Short-term capital gains on immovable property
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.2(42A) and the general charging provision; short-term capital gains are added to total income and taxed at the applicable slab.
holdingPeriodRule: 24 months or less.
taxRate: Slab rates. Because the gain is added to total income, it can push other income into higher slabs.
exemptionLimit: None directly. Short-term gains may be eligible for s.54B relief only in the case of agricultural land used for two years immediately before transfer.
surchargeRule: Surcharge determined by total income on the ordinary scale, not capped at 15%, because the income is not taxed under s.111A, s.112 or s.112A.
setOffRule: Short-term capital loss on property may be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains.
conditions: Transfer expenditure is deductible.
Since the gain is taxed at slab rates, the marginal-rate effect must be modelled: a large short-term property gain can raise the effective rate on the taxpayer's other income.

title: Specified mutual funds acquired on or after 1 April 2023 — deemed short-term, slab rates
assetClass: Debt mutual funds, market-linked debentures, unlisted bonds and debentures
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.50AA.
holdingPeriodRule: Holding period is irrelevant. Where a specified mutual fund or market-linked debenture is acquired on or after 1 April 2023, the gain is always deemed short-term regardless of how long it is held.
taxRate: Applicable slab rate, with no indexation benefit. The gain is added to total income.
exemptionLimit: None. The basic exemption threshold may absorb part of the gain if the taxpayer has no other income.
surchargeRule: Ordinary surcharge scale, since the gain is not taxed under s.111A, s.112 or s.112A.
setOffRule: Deemed short-term capital loss may be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains.
conditions: The provision applies to units of a specified mutual fund where not more than 35% of proceeds are invested in equity shares of domestic companies.
It also applies to market-linked debentures and to unlisted bonds and debentures.
For units acquired before 1 April 2023, the pre-amendment regime applies, with the post-July-2024 rates applied on transfer.
workedExampleSummary: Acquired April 2023 for ₹10,00,000; sold in FY 2025-26 for ₹18,00,000. Gains of ₹8,00,000 are deemed short-term. Assuming no other income and the new regime, the ₹4,00,000 basic exemption absorbs part of the gain and the balance is taxed at slab rates.
notes: This is the provision that ended the practice of treating long-duration debt funds as an indexation-based capital-gains vehicle. Arthanomy treats it as the single most consequential change to Indian debt-fund taxation in a decade.

title: Debt mutual fund units acquired before 1 April 2023 — grandfathering under the pre-amendment regime
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.112 read with the transitional provisions created by the Finance Act 2023 amendment of s.50AA.
holdingPeriodRule: At least 24 months for long-term treatment on units acquired before 1 April 2023.
taxRate: 12.5% without indexation for long-term gains; slab rates for short-term gains. Indexation is not available for transfers on or after 23 July 2024.
exemptionLimit: None for this asset class; the ₹1,25,000 exemption applies to s.112A assets only.
surchargeRule: 15% cap for long-term gains taxed under s.112.
setOffRule: Standard capital-loss sequencing applies.
conditions: Vintage of acquisition, not the date of sale, determines which regime applies.
Units acquired before 1 April 2023 remain grandfathered for holding-period purposes.
notes: This rule exists specifically to keep historical treatment visible. A reader holding pre-2023 units must not apply the s.50AA slab treatment to the whole holding period. Brokers and registrar statements normally part-identify holdings by acquisition lot for this reason.

title: Long-term capital gains on other assets (gold, unlisted shares, jewellery, foreign assets)
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.112.
holdingPeriodRule: More than 24 months for unlisted shares, gold, jewellery and most other capital assets.
taxRate: 12.5% without indexation and, for non-residents, without the first proviso currency-translation benefit.
exemptionLimit: None, except where a specific provision applies (for example the s.54F reinvestment route for assets other than a residential house).
surchargeRule: Surcharge capped at 15% for s.112 income.
setOffRule: Long-term capital losses may be set off only against long-term capital gains.
conditions: Notified gold bonds and certain sovereign instruments have separate exemptions.
The s.54F route requires investment of the net consideration in a residential house and carries a proportionate-exemption formula.
Unlisted bonds and debentures are covered by s.50AA if acquired on or after 1 April 2023 and are therefore excluded from this rule for post-April-2023 acquisitions.
notes: The removal of indexation for long-duration assets materially worsened the post-tax outcome of physical gold holding, jewellery purchase as an investment, and unlisted-share investment for high-inflation periods. Articles that compare gold vehicles must reflect this.

title: Sovereign Gold Bond — interest and redemption treatment
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.10(15)(vi) and s.47(viic), together with the terms of each tranche notified by the Government.
holdingPeriodRule: The bond has a tenure set by the tranche (typically eight years) with an exit option after the fifth year on interest-payment dates. Redemption by a resident individual at maturity is not treated as a transfer under s.47(viic).
taxRate: Interest at 2.50% per annum (tranche-dependent) is taxable at the applicable slab rate. Capital gains on redemption by an individual at maturity are exempt under s.47(viic). Gains on a sale in the secondary market are taxable.
exemptionLimit: Redemption by an individual at maturity is exempt; secondary-market transfers are not.
surchargeRule: Applies to interest as ordinary income at the ordinary scale.
setOffRule: Losses on secondary-market transfers follow ordinary capital-loss rules.
conditions: The s.47(viic) exemption applies to redemption by an individual, and the exemption does not extend to a trust, firm or company.
The exemption applies to redemption at maturity; an early exit through the RBI window after year five and a secondary-market sale are treated differently.
TCS has historically applied to cash purchases of SGB above a monetary threshold — that threshold has changed between Finance Acts and must be checked for the year in question.
Issue price, coupon and tranche availability are tranche-specific facts, not permanent features of the product.
productStatus: Arthanomy does not assert that Sovereign Gold Bonds are currently open for subscription. Whether a new tranche is being issued, and whether existing tranches are available in the secondary market at a particular price, are separate and time-sensitive questions that must be verified against current RBI releases and exchange listings.
notes: Marked provisional because the exemption's interaction with secondary-market sales, the TCS threshold and the current issuance programme all change over time and have not all been re-verified for Tax Year 2026-27.

title: Gold ETFs, gold funds and physical gold — capital gains treatment
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.112. Gold ETFs and gold fund-of-funds that do not satisfy the 65% domestic-equity test are not s.112A assets.
holdingPeriodRule: More than 24 months for long-term treatment. This is the point most often misreported: gold ETFs and gold funds-of-funds are not treated as listed equity for capital-gains purposes.
taxRate: Long-term: 12.5% without indexation. Short-term: slab rates.
exemptionLimit: None. The s.112A ₹1,25,000 exemption does not apply.
surchargeRule: 15% cap for long-term gains under s.112; ordinary scale for short-term gains taxed at slab.
setOffRule: Standard sequencing; short-term losses more flexible than long-term losses.
conditions: Physical gold: jewellery and coins are capital assets; the acquisition cost must be evidenced. Inherited gold requires the previous owner's cost and the date from which the previous owner held it.

Gold monetisation scheme deposits and gold deposit certificates are specifically excluded from the definition of capital assets in certain cases — this should be confirmed for the specific scheme before relying on it.
Making charges paid on jewellery form part of the cost of acquisition, which reduces the taxable gain but does not recover the economic loss on resale.
notes: Because gold ETFs must be held more than 24 months for long-term treatment while listed equity needs only 12 months, a reader comparing an equity position and a gold position of identical vintages pays different rates on identical gains.

title: Virtual digital assets — flat 30% taxation with no loss set-off
assetClass: Crypto assets and virtual digital assets
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.115BBH read with s.194S for tax deduction at source.
holdingPeriodRule: Holding period is irrelevant for the special rate. Any gain on transfer of a virtual digital asset is taxed at the flat rate below, regardless of how long it was held.
taxRate: 30% flat on the gain, plus surcharge and cess, with no deduction other than the cost of acquisition. No expense deduction is permitted, and no indexation.
exemptionLimit: None. The basic exemption threshold cannot be applied against this income in the manner that applies to ordinary slab income, and losses cannot be set off against any other head or against other VDA gains.
surchargeRule: Surcharge applies on the ordinary scale; the 15% cap that applies to s.111A, s.112 and s.112A income does not extend to s.115BBH income.
setOffRule: Losses from the transfer of a virtual digital asset cannot be set off against gains from another virtual digital asset or against any other income, and cannot be carried forward.
conditions: Gifts of virtual digital assets are taxable in the recipient's hands under the gift provisions, and the giver receives no deduction.
Tax is deducted at source at 1% on transfer consideration above the applicable threshold under s.194S.
Airdrops and certain receipt events are treated as income from other sources, taxed at the slab rate as the case may be, with a different computation basis from a sale gain.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 explicitly covers virtual digital assets and, on the secondary reporting available to Arthanomy, does not change the manner of taxation.
notes: Marked provisional because the treatment of specific events (staking rewards, hard forks, DeFi yield, airdrops) has been the subject of evolving guidance and Arthanomy has not verified a primary circular for each event type.

title: Dividend income and dividend tax deduction at source
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — dividend is taxable in the shareholder's hands as income from other sources, with tax deduction at source under s.194.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable; dividend is taxed when received or declared payable, not on a holding-period basis.
taxRate: Applicable slab rate on the gross dividend, with the cost of earning the dividend generally not deductible except for interest expense incurred to earn it, subject to limits.
exemptionLimit: Tax deduction at source applies only above the statutory threshold for the year. The threshold is a compliance threshold, not an exemption from tax: dividend below the threshold remains fully taxable and must be reported.
surchargeRule: Ordinary surcharge scale. Dividend income is, however, subject to the 15% surcharge cap where the enhanced rates would otherwise apply — a rule that changed with effect from 1 April 2020 and should be re-verified for the year in question.
setOffRule: Interest expense incurred to earn dividend income can be deducted, but only to the extent of dividend income, and the excess cannot be carried forward.
conditions: The dividend distribution tax previously paid by companies was abolished with effect from 1 April 2020; historical articles that quote dividend distribution tax are describing a repealed regime.
Because dividend is taxed at slab rates, a high-income investor in the 30% slab plus surcharge and cess can retain materially less than the headline dividend yield.

title: Bank and post-office deposit interest
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — interest is taxable under 'Income from other sources'; tax deduction at source under s.194A; deduction under s.80TTA or s.80TTB in the old regime.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable. Interest is taxed on accrual or receipt, according to the method of accounting, regardless of whether the deposit has matured.
taxRate: Slab rates. Fixed-deposit interest is fully taxable; there is no special rate.
exemptionLimit: s.80TTA allows a deduction of up to ₹10,000 of savings-account interest for a non-senior resident in the old regime. s.80TTB allows up to ₹50,000 of interest on deposits for a resident senior citizen in the old regime. Neither deduction is available in the new regime.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale.
setOffRule: Interest paid on a loan taken to invest in a deposit can be deducted against that interest income where the borrowing is for the purpose of earning the income, subject to the specific provision and limits.
conditions: TDS applies to interest above the statutory threshold for the payer type; a senior citizen can file a declaration to avoid deduction where tax is not ultimately payable.
Banks report accrued interest on a cumulative deposit annually even though cash has not been received — the tax is payable on the accrual, which is a genuine cash-flow trap in cumulative deposits.
Deposit insurance covers each depositor per bank up to the statutory ceiling; the ceiling has changed and must be checked. Co-operative banks and non-bank deposit-takers have different arrangements.

title: Peer-to-peer lending interest, losses and tax deduction at source
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — interest from a loan is taxable under 'Income from other sources' or, where lending is a business activity, under 'Profits and gains of business or profession'. Tax deduction at source on interest paid by the platform is under s.194BA.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable. Interest is taxable on accrual or receipt basis, and capital-loss treatment is not available because a loan is not a capital asset in the borrower's hands.
taxRate: Slab rates, at the taxpayer's marginal rate.
exemptionLimit: None. Unlike a dividend or a capital gain, lending interest receives no concessional rate and no exemption threshold.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale. Because interest is ordinary income, it can trigger the 25% or 37% enhanced surcharge bands at high total income, which is a materially worse outcome than the 15%-capped capital-gains route.
setOffRule: Arthanomy's position: a principal loss on a defaulted loan is generally a loss on a current asset or a bad debt rather than a capital loss. Whether it is deductible depends on whether the lending constitutes a business, whether the specific debt has become irrecoverable, and the applicable provision. This question is genuinely contested for retail lenders and depends on facts; a reader should get advice rather than assume deductibility. Booked-but-unreceived interest must not be assumed to be loss-deductible merely because the platform reports an overdue balance.
conditions: Interest is taxable when it accrues or is received according to the taxpayer's method of accounting. Platforms that credit accrued interest to an account receivable will typically generate a tax liability before any cash is recovered.

Tax is deducted at source on interest credited or paid in respect of a P2P loan from 1 April 2023 under s.194BA. The interaction between platform-level deduction and the investor's own filing makes reconciliation with the annual information statement important.
Because returns are reported by platforms on a gross interest basis while defaults are reported separately, the taxable figure for a given year can exceed the cash actually received.
notes: Marked provisional because the deductibility of principal losses for non-business retail lenders is not settled by any provision Arthanomy has been able to verify with certainty, and because the s.194BA mechanics interact with platform-level reporting that varies by platform. Arthanomy states the uncertainty rather than resolving it.

title: REIT and InvIT distributions — component-wise taxation
incomeType: Interest, dividend and repayment of capital
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — s.10(23FD) and related provisions for distributions from business trusts; the Finance Act 2020 removed the exemption for the dividend component, and s.194LBA governs tax deduction at source.
holdingPeriodRule: Units of a business trust held more than 12 months qualify as long-term capital assets, so the capital-gains holding period follows the listed-equity convention rather than the 24-month convention.
taxRate: Distribution is taxed component-wise: the interest component is taxable at slab rates as income from other sources; the dividend component is taxable at slab rates; and the repayment-of-debt component is treated as a return of capital, reducing the unit holder's cost of acquisition and therefore increasing the eventual capital gain or reducing the loss. Capital gains on sale are taxed under the s.111A/s.112A framework, so the ₹1,25,000 exemption and the 12.5% long-term rate can apply.
exemptionLimit: The ₹1,25,000 annual exemption applies to long-term capital gains on units, subject to securities transaction tax being paid on the transfer.
surchargeRule: The distribution components are taxed as ordinary income with the ordinary surcharge scale; capital gains on units are subject to the 15% cap.
setOffRule: Standard sequencing. Note that a return-of-capital component is not a loss and cannot be claimed as one; it only reduces the cost base.
conditions: The headline distribution yield is not the taxable return. A distribution can be partly a return of the investor's own capital.
Tax is deducted at source under s.194LBA to the extent the distribution is taxable.
Because the dividend component became taxable from 1 April 2020, articles written before that date materially understate the tax cost of REIT distributions.
The characterisation of each component is reported by the trust and must be taken from the trust's own distribution statement, not inferred from the headline yield.
notes: This is a common source of overstated after-tax yields in Indian real-estate commentary: a high distribution yield that is materially a return of capital is not comparable with an interest coupon.

title: Employee stock options and restricted stock units — perquisite and capital gains
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — s.17(2)(vi) treats the difference between the fair market value on the date of exercise and the amount paid by the employee as a perquisite; s.191(2A) addresses the responsible payer; the Finance Act 2020 introduced an eligible-start-up deferral.
holdingPeriodRule: For capital gains, the holding period for listed shares begins on the date of allotment — but the date from which the asset is 'held' for cost purposes can differ between the perquisite moment and the capital-gains moment.
taxRate: At exercise, the perquisite is taxed at slab rates as salary income with tax deducted at source by the employer. On sale, the gain over the perquisite-inclusive cost is taxed as a capital gain: 20% short-term under s.111A or 12.5% long-term under s.112A above the ₹1,25,000 exemption.
exemptionLimit: ₹1,25,000 annual exemption on long-term capital gains only.
surchargeRule: Slab-rate surcharge on the perquisite; the 15% cap on the capital-gains leg.
setOffRule: Standard sequencing for the capital-gains leg.
conditions: The perquisite is calculated on the fair market value on the date of exercise for a listed company, and the cost base for the subsequent sale is the perquisite value plus the exercise price paid.

Double taxation of the same economic amount is avoided by adding the perquisite to the cost of acquisition, but only if the employer's tax-deduction and reporting are correctly reflected in the annual information statement.
Where the shares are unlisted, the perquisite valuation follows a prescribed method and the resulting shares are unlisted capital assets with a 24-month long-term threshold.
The eligible-start-up deferral under s.191(2A) postpones the tax point; it does not reduce the tax.

Where the shares fall below the exercise price after tax has been paid on the perquisite, the employee bears a real economic loss on an amount on which tax has already been paid. Arthanomy treats this as the central risk of employee equity and quantifies it with the ESOP payoff calculator.

title: Share buyback taxation
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — the buyback distribution is treated as dividend income in the shareholder's hands under s.2(22)(f), with the company required to withhold tax under s.194. The tax previously paid by the company on buyback was withdrawn with effect from 1 October 2024.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable to the buyback consideration itself, which is taxed as dividend. However, the cost of the shares bought back is treated as a capital loss, since the shares are extinguished.
taxRate: Slab rates on the gross buyback consideration, because it is deemed dividend.
exemptionLimit: None.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale, subject to the dividend-related surcharge cap where applicable.
setOffRule: The cost of acquisition of the shares bought back is treated as a capital loss in the year of the buyback. Whether it is short-term or long-term depends on the holding period of the shares, and it follows the ordinary set-off sequencing.
conditions: The effective date of the change was 1 October 2024; the previous regime, under which the company bore the buyback tax, applied to buybacks completed before that date.

Because the gross consideration is taxed at slab rates while the cost is recovered only as a capital loss, the cash-flow and rate mismatch can materially reduce the after-tax outcome relative to selling in the market, and the two routes must be compared explicitly.

A tender-offer buyback in a market with an acceptance ratio has an additional economic cost that is unrelated to tax: the shares not accepted retain their position and the investor's post-issue exposure is not what was intended.
notes: Marked provisional because the precise interaction between the deemed-dividend treatment and the capital-loss characterisation of the extinguished cost has been the subject of professional debate and Arthanomy has not verified a single authoritative circular settling every fact pattern.

title: Taxation of gifts received and given
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.56(2)(x) for gifts of money and property.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable; the taxation is on receipt. For a subsequently sold gifted asset, the holding period includes the period for which the previous owner held it, and the cost of acquisition is the previous owner's cost, with an exception for certain assets received by gift where the previous owner's cost is used.
taxRate: Slab rates in the recipient's hands to the extent the aggregate value of gifts received in the year exceeds ₹50,000.
exemptionLimit: Gifts are exempt where received from a relative, on the occasion of marriage, under a will or inheritance, in contemplation of death, or from specified institutions, without a value limit.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale.
setOffRule: Gift income is not eligible for capital-loss set-off.
conditions: The ₹50,000 threshold applies to the aggregate of gifts received from all non-exempt sources in the financial year.

Where the aggregate does not exceed ₹50,000, the full amount is exempt; where it exceeds ₹50,000, the entire amount received from non-exempt sources is taxable, not merely the excess — a step-function that is commonly misunderstood.

A gift of shares or property to a relative is exempt in the recipient's hands, but the relative's cost base for a future sale is the donor's cost, so the capital-gains liability is preserved rather than eliminated.
Gifting to a spouse does not by itself shift the tax base where the income is subsequently earned on the transferred asset; clubbing provisions can apply.

title: Liberalised Remittance Scheme and tax collection at source on foreign remittances
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.206C(1G); Foreign Exchange Management Act and the RBI Master Direction on the Liberalised Remittance Scheme.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable to the collection itself. Remittance under LRS creates the foreign asset; the asset's own holding-period rules then apply for capital gains.
taxRate: Tax is collected at source at the prescribed rate on the remittance amount above the prescribed threshold, with different rates for investment remittances and for education or medical remittances, and with a lower rate where the funds are from a loan and a higher rate above a specified monetary threshold.
exemptionLimit: A basic threshold applies below which collection does not arise. The threshold and the rates were revised by successive Finance Acts and the figures currently in force must be confirmed for the specific financial year before any reference.
surchargeRule: Not applicable to the collection, which is a form of advance tax. It is creditable against the taxpayer's final liability.
cessRule: Not applicable to the collection itself.
setOffRule: Not applicable. The collected amount is adjusted against the total tax liability for the year.
conditions: LRS is subject to an annual monetary limit per person per financial year, which has been revised over time.
Tax collected at source is not an additional tax; it is a prepayment creditable against the final liability. It does, however, create a real cash-flow cost between remittance and filing.
The rate applicable to an investment remittance differs from the rate applicable to education and medical remittances.

Foreign assets acquired must be disclosed in the relevant schedule of the income-tax return where the taxpayer is a resident and ordinarily resident. Non-disclosure carries consequences under the Black Money Act regime, which is materially more severe than ordinary under-reporting.
notes: Marked provisional on rates and thresholds, which have changed repeatedly and could not be re-verified from a primary source at the time of writing. The structure of the rule — collection at source, creditable, distinct rates by purpose — is stable.

title: Taxation of foreign equity shares and overseas funds held by a resident
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.112 for long-term gains and the general charging provisions for dividend; relief under an applicable double-taxation avoidance agreement under s.90 or s.90A, claimed by filing the prescribed form.
holdingPeriodRule: More than 24 months for unlisted foreign shares and for most overseas fund units. Directly listed foreign shares are unlisted for Indian tax purposes unless specifically covered, so the 24-month threshold applies rather than 12 months.
taxRate: 12.5% without indexation on long-term gains; slab rates on short-term gains; dividend at slab rates. There is no s.112A treatment for foreign shares, so no ₹1,25,000 exemption applies.
exemptionLimit: None for foreign assets.
surchargeRule: 15% cap for long-term gains under s.112; ordinary scale for dividend.
setOffRule: Standard sequencing. Foreign losses should be modelled separately from Indian losses, since a treaty may restrict relief.
conditions: Foreign tax credit requires timely filing of the prescribed statement and a certificate from the foreign tax authority. It is not automatic.
The double-taxation relief can be claimed under the agreement or under the unilateral relief provision, and the two are not identical in effect.
Foreign asset disclosure obligations apply to a resident and ordinarily resident. Failure to disclose is governed by a separate and much harsher penalty regime than ordinary under-reporting.
Dividends from foreign companies are generally taxed at slab rates in India, with treaty relief for foreign withholding where available.

Where an Indian mutual fund invests abroad, the Indian fund's unit is an Indian asset and is taxed under the Indian fund's own characterisation, which is different from holding the foreign asset directly.
notes: Arthanomy treats 'an Indian fund that invests abroad' and 'an overseas asset held directly' as different tax objects and never conflates them.

title: National Pension System — contribution, accrual, withdrawal and annuity taxation
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.80CCD(1), s.80CCD(1B) and s.80CCD(2); s.10(12A) and s.10(12B) for partial and full withdrawals.
holdingPeriodRule: Locked until 60 to exit for the annuity portion; partial withdrawal is permitted for specified purposes after a minimum tier-1 contribution period.
taxRate: Deduction under s.80CCD(1) within the overall s.80C-type ceiling, an additional ₹50,000 under s.80CCD(1B) — both available only under the old regime — and an employer contribution deduction under s.80CCD(2) that is available in the new regime and is the single most valuable NPS-related deduction for a salaried taxpayer. At exit, up to a specified share of the corpus must be annuitised and the balance is received as a lump sum; the lump-sum portion is exempt under s.10(12A) subject to conditions, and annuity income is taxable at slab rates as it is received.
exemptionLimit: The lump-sum share at exit is exempt subject to conditions; annuity income is not exempt.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale for annuity income; deductions reduce the base before surcharge.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: Because annuity income is fully taxable at slab while the lump-sum portion is exempt subject to conditions, an NPS exit in a high-income year is materially worse than in a low-income year. This is a sequencing decision, not a product decision.
NPS Tier-1 has a longer lock-in than most investors expect and the annuity requirement is mandatory, so NPS is not a substitute for a liquid debt allocation.
The employer-contribution deduction under s.80CCD(2) is available even in the default new regime, which makes corporate NPS a rare deduction that survives the regime switch.
Asset-allocation caps between equity, corporate debt, government securities and alternative assets are set by PFRDA and vary by the active or auto choice selected.
notes: Arthanomy does not display a current NPS contribution limit for the corporate deduction without confirming the applicable percentage of salary, which differs between government and non-government employers.

title: Public Provident Fund — exempt-exempt-exempt treatment
provision: Public Provident Fund Act, 1968 and the scheme rules; income-tax treatment under s.10(11) for the accumulated balance and s.80C for contributions in the old regime.
holdingPeriodRule: 15 years from the end of the financial year of opening, with permitted extension in five-year blocks with or without further contribution.
taxRate: Exempt-exempt-exempt: contributions qualify for s.80C deduction in the old regime, interest accrues free of tax, and maturity proceeds are exempt. The exempt treatment of interest and maturity is available in both regimes; only the deduction on contribution is confined to the old regime.
exemptionLimit: The statutory maximum annual deposit applies; deposits above it earn no interest and are not eligible for deduction.
surchargeRule: Not applicable to the exempt interest and maturity amounts.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: The interest rate is administratively reset each quarter by the Finance Ministry against a formula linked to government securities yields, so any quoted rate is a point-in-time figure and not a forecast.
Partial withdrawal is permitted only under specified conditions and after a minimum period.
No deposit is permitted in a year without incurring a penalty (historically a fixed minimum annual deposit), so a lapse has a small but real cost.

Since interest is exempt, PPF is more valuable to a taxpayer in a high slab than the headline rate suggests, and less valuable to a taxpayer with no other income whose alternative would also be tax-free.
notes: Arthanomy deliberately does not display a current PPF interest rate. The rate is reset quarterly by administrative decision and quoting it without the applicable quarter would be misleading.

title: Employees' Provident Fund — contributions, interest and withdrawal
provision: Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952; income-tax treatment under s.10(11) and s.10(12) for the accumulated balance, with the taxation of interest on contributions above a threshold introduced by the Finance Act 2021.
holdingPeriodRule: Continuous employment-linked; withdrawal before five years of continuous service attracts tax on the accumulated balance including the employer's share, subject to exceptions.
taxRate: The accumulated balance is exempt on five years of continuous service, subject to the annual monetary threshold for a recognised provident fund. Interest attributable to an employee's own contributions above the threshold became taxable, and the mechanism to compute that interest is administratively prescribed. Contributions qualify for s.80C in the old regime; the employer's contribution above the statutory limit is a taxable perquisite in specified circumstances.
exemptionLimit: The accumulated balance exemption applies on completion of five years of continuous service and in certain specified cases of earlier cessation, including ill health.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale on taxable portions.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: Five years of continuous service is the operative test, not five calendar years of membership, and the exceptions matter.

Because the taxable-interest computation requires the employee to compute interest attributable to their own high-balance contributions, the practical difficulty of the calculation is itself a reason to keep the necessary records.
Tax deducted at source on a premature withdrawal applies where the balance is taxable.
The EPF interest rate is administratively determined each year and is not a market rate.
notes: Marked provisional on the current monetary thresholds for the interest-taxation mechanism, which Arthanomy has not re-verified for the current year. The five-year rule and the basic tax treatment of the accumulated balance are stable.

title: Sukanya Samriddhi Account — eligibility, limits and tax treatment
provision: Sukanya Samriddhi Account Scheme, 2019 and the Government Savings Promotion Act regime; s.10(11A) for the exemption of the accumulated balance.
holdingPeriodRule: Twenty-one years from the date of opening, with deposits permitted for fifteen years; the account matures at the end of twenty-one years unless closed earlier on the permitted conditions.
taxRate: Exempt-exempt-exempt treatment: contributions qualify for s.80C in the old regime, interest accrues free of tax, and the maturity proceeds are exempt where the conditions are satisfied.
exemptionLimit: A statutory minimum and maximum annual deposit apply. The maximum is administratively set and has changed over time.
surchargeRule: Not applicable to the exempt amounts.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: The account is opened for a daughter and the depositor must be a parent or legal guardian, limited to two accounts per family under the scheme rules subject to the exceptions stated in the rules.

The 15-year deposit window and the 21-year maturity mean part of the account simply compounds without further deposits after year fifteen — which raises the effective duration of the last deposits well above fifteen years.
Partial withdrawal for education is permitted only on the conditions and after the minimum age stated in the rules.
The interest rate is administratively reset quarterly, so any rate quoted is a point-in-time value.

title: Life insurance maturity proceeds — s.10(10D) exemption and its limits
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.10(10D).
holdingPeriodRule: Not a holding-period test. The test is the relationship between the annual premium and the sum assured, and whether the policy is a unit-linked or non-linked product.
taxRate: Maturity proceeds are exempt where the annual premium does not exceed the prescribed percentage of the sum assured. For policies issued on or after 1 April 2023, a monetary cap on the aggregate annual premium applies for the exemption: proceeds attributable to premiums above the cap become taxable. The exemption is separately restricted for unit-linked policies where the aggregate annual premium exceeds the specified threshold, and the taxable portion is treated as a capital gain.
exemptionLimit: The structure is a premium-to-sum-assured ratio test plus, for recent vintages, a monetary premium cap. The specific percentages and caps are vintage-dependent and differ for policies issued before and after the Finance Act 2023 changes, with a further tightening for policies issued on or after 1 October 2024.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale on the taxable portion.
setOffRule: Standard sequencing for the capital-gains portion of a unit-linked taxable amount.
conditions: The exemptions are policy-vintage dependent. A generic statement that 'life insurance maturity is tax-free under s.10(10D)' is inaccurate for large premium policies issued recently.

Traditional endowment and money-back products typically combine a small insurance component with a low-yield savings component. Arthanomy analyses them by separating the mortality charge from the savings return rather than treating the maturity value as an investment return.

Surrender before maturity usually converts a policy into a capital gain or loss with a different computation basis, and surrender values in the early years of a traditional policy are typically well below cumulative premiums paid.
notes: Marked provisional on the exact premium caps and ratio thresholds, which differ by policy vintage and product type and which Arthanomy has not re-verified for every vintage. The direction of the rule — recent large-premium policies are no longer automatically exempt — is confirmed.

title: Unit-linked insurance plans — charges, taxation and the cost of the insurance wrapper
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.10(10D) with the s.112A-equivalent treatment for taxable unit-linked proceeds; IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations for charge and discontinuance rules.
holdingPeriodRule: For the taxable portion, the equity-oriented unit-linked test and the 12-month threshold apply.
taxRate: Within the exemption, proceeds are exempt. Where the premium cap is exceeded, the gain is taxable; where the underlying fund is equity-oriented, the s.112A-type treatment at 12.5% above the ₹1,25,000 exemption can apply, and non-equity-oriented unit-linked gains follow the corresponding capital-gains treatment.
exemptionLimit: Vintage-dependent premium caps as described in the life-insurance rule.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale for taxable portions, with the 15% cap where the gains fall under the capital-gains provisions.
setOffRule: Capital-gains sequencing where the gain is taxable.
conditions: Because the wrapper carries mortality and administration charges in addition to fund-management charges, a unit-linked plan's net return is lower than the same underlying portfolio held directly, and the gap widens over short holding periods.

Charge caps are regulated, but the caps are ceilings rather than a description of what a particular product charges; the actual charges must be read from the benefit illustration and the policy document.
Mortality charges rise with age, so the drag increases over the life of the policy — the opposite of the direction in which a mutual fund expense ratio typically moves.
Loyalty additions, where offered, are conditional and are typically forfeited on early exit, which makes the headline illustration sensitive to a full-term assumption.

title: Annuity income and pension products
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — annuity received under a life insurance policy is taxable as income from other sources under s.56, with the treatment of a purchased annuity depending on the portion representing return of capital.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable; annuity is taxed as it is received.
taxRate: Where the annuity is a return of the purchase price, a portion of each payment may represent return of capital rather than income, depending on the product and the option selected. Immediate annuities purchased with capital typically involve a capital-recovery element for a term certain or for a return-of-premium variant.
exemptionLimit: None; annuity income is not exempt.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: Because the nominal annuity rate is applied to the original purchase price while the real value of each payment is eroded by inflation, the real internal rate of return on a level immediate annuity is materially lower than the headline annuity rate, and for long durations it can be negative in real terms.
A joint-life annuity with a return-of-premium option pays a lower rate than a life-only annuity on a single life, and the difference is the price of the survivor and capital-protection features.
Annuity rates are age-dependent and were materially higher during high-rate periods. A rate quoted in one year is not a permanent property of the product.
notes: Arthanomy uses this rule with the real-return and break-even inflation calculators, because the central question about an annuity is not the nominal rate but the break-even inflation rate at which the real return goes to zero.

title: Derivatives and intraday trading — business income treatment and loss rules
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — s.43(5) excludes certain derivative transactions from the definition of speculative transaction; s.72 and s.73 govern the set-off of business losses, and s.74 governs speculation business losses.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable. Derivative and intraday gains are not capital gains; the holding period does not determine the treatment.
taxRate: Slab rates on net trading profit, with the ordinary surcharge scale and 4% cess. Because it is business income, the surcharge can reach 25% or 37%, unlike capital gains which are capped at 15%.
exemptionLimit: None.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale; the enhanced rates apply at high total income.
setOffRule: A loss from a non-speculative derivatives business can be set off against other business income and, subject to conditions, against other heads in the same year, and can be carried forward for up to eight assessment years against business income. A loss from a speculative business — which includes intraday equity trading — can be set off only against speculative business income in the same year and carried forward only against speculative business income. This distinction is the single most consequential tax fact for a retail trader and is frequently misunderstood.
conditions: Derivative transactions on a recognised stock exchange are excluded from the definition of speculative transaction, while intraday equity trading that is settled otherwise than by delivery is speculative business income.
Where derivatives trading is a business, books of account, audit and advance-tax obligations can arise depending on turnover and the applicable presumptive provisions.
Turnover computation for derivatives differs from the value of contracts, and the applicable method materially affects audit thresholds.
Tax audit and presumptive-provision interaction: a taxpayer who has a trading loss may face an audit question where income is declared below the presumptive rate in a later year.
Losses must be reported in the return filed by the due date to be carried forward.
notes: Marked provisional on the turnover-computation method and audit thresholds applicable to derivative traders in the current year, which depend on specific provisions and guidance that Arthanomy has not individually re-verified.

title: Set-off and carry-forward of capital losses
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.70 (intra-head set-off), s.71 (inter-head set-off) and s.74 (carry-forward of capital losses).
holdingPeriodRule: Determined by the holding period of the asset that produced the loss.
taxRate: Not applicable; this rule governs the loss, not the income.
exemptionLimit: Not applicable.
surchargeRule: Not applicable.
setOffRule: A short-term capital loss may be set off against both short-term capital gains and long-term capital gains in the same year. A long-term capital loss may be set off only against long-term capital gains. Unabsorbed capital losses may be carried forward for up to eight assessment years, and the character of the loss (short-term or long-term) is preserved in the carry-forward. Carry-forward requires the return to be filed by the due date under s.139(1); a belated return loses the carry-forward even if the loss is disclosed.
conditions: A s.112A loss cannot be set off against gains that are not eligible for the s.112A rate. The gain must be of the same character.
Losses from a virtual digital asset cannot be set off or carried forward at all — a specific carve-out that overrides the general framework.

Long-term capital loss on a s.112A asset can be set off against long-term s.112A gains and, where the same asset class produces it, against other s.112A gains; the sequencing should be checked for each fact pattern.
Carry-forward requires the return by the due date; the loss set-off within the same year does not require a timely return.
The limitation on loss set-off applies to the character of the gain: a s.112A long-term loss cannot be set against a non-112A long-term gain.
notes: The requirement to file by the due date to preserve a carry-forward is the reason tax-loss harvesting must be planned before the year-end rather than considered in the following April.

title: Advance tax instalments and interest for shortfall
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.207 to s.211 for the obligation and instalment schedule, and s.234B and s.234C for interest on default.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Interest at the prescribed rate per month or part-month for shortfall in instalments and for failure to pay the balance before the year-end, computed on the assessed tax less tax deducted or collected at source.
exemptionLimit: A monetary threshold below which advance tax is not required; and a resident senior citizen with no business income is exempt from the obligation.
surchargeRule: Not applicable.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: Instalments fall due at prescribed percentages on 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March.

Capital gains are treated differently from ordinary income: a taxpayer cannot reasonably estimate a gain that has not yet occurred, so interest is generally computed on the basis that capital gains are treated as income of the quarter in which they arise for the purpose of the instalment in which they are included.
Tax deducted or collected at source is creditable, which can eliminate the obligation for a salaried taxpayer whose entire income is subject to withholding.

Because a large one-off capital gain can trigger a shortfall in the quarter it arises, the practical implication is that a taxpayer who realises a large gain in the last quarter should pay the resulting advance tax on or before 15 March rather than waiting for the return.
Interest for default is charged at a fixed rate per month, which makes the effective cost of deferring a known liability a calculable number rather than an unknown penalty.
notes: Advance-tax interest is one of the few tax costs that is entirely avoidable with planning, and the domain it most often affects is a mid-year equity sale or a property sale.

title: Surcharge bands and marginal relief
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — surcharge on income tax at the rates specified for the relevant total-income band, with a cap on the rate applicable to s.111A, s.112 and s.112A income and to dividend income.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Nil up to ₹50 lakh; 10% on the portion of tax where total income exceeds ₹50 lakh; 15% above ₹1 crore; 25% above ₹2 crore; and above ₹5 crore, 25% under the new regime or 37% under the old regime. The 25% and 37% rates do not apply to income chargeable under s.111A, s.112 or s.112A, or to dividend income, where the maximum surcharge is 15%.
exemptionLimit: Marginal relief applies at each band boundary so that the tax plus surcharge on income just above a threshold does not exceed the tax on the threshold income plus the amount by which income exceeds the threshold.
surchargeRule: This rule is itself the surcharge rule.
cessRule: Health and education cess at 4% of income tax plus surcharge.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: The 15% cap is one of the strongest tax arguments in favour of a long-term equity capital-gains route over an interest-bearing route for a high-income investor: interest income faces a surcharge rising to 25% or 37%, whereas long-term equity gains face a maximum of 15%.
Marginal relief must be computed at each band boundary and is not the same as reducing the surcharge rate.
The old regime retains the 37% top rate while the new regime caps at 25%, which is a material difference for very high income earners and is part of the regime comparison.

title: Health and education cess
provision: Finance Act — cess levied on income tax plus surcharge.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: 4% of income tax plus surcharge, in both regimes.
exemptionLimit: Not applicable.
surchargeRule: Not applicable; cess is computed after surcharge.
cessRule: This rule is itself the cess rule.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: Cess is not creditable against any other tax and cannot be refunded other than as part of a refund of the underlying tax.

The 4% cess must be included in every effective-rate calculation; omitting it understates the tax cost by approximately 4% of the tax, or roughly 1.2 to 1.4 percentage points at the top marginal rate.

title: Securities transaction tax, stamp duty and exchange transaction charges
provision: Finance Act provisions levying securities transaction tax; the Indian Stamp Act as amended for uniform securities-market stamp duty collected by the exchange or depository; exchange transaction charges as published by each exchange.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Securities transaction tax is levied at rates that differ by instrument and by side of the transaction — equity delivery, intraday, futures and options carry different rates, and the options rate applies to the premium rather than to the notional. Stamp duty is levied on the buy side for most instruments at rates that differ by instrument. Exchange transaction charges are levied on turnover at relatively low rates.
exemptionLimit: Not applicable.
surchargeRule: Not applicable.
setOffRule: Securities transaction tax is specifically not deductible as an expense in computing capital gains, even though it is an unavoidable transaction cost. It therefore reduces the economic return but cannot be claimed against the gain. Brokerage and exchange charges are generally deductible as transfer expenditure, subject to the specific provision.
conditions: Securities transaction tax must have been paid on a transfer for s.111A and s.112A treatment to apply.
For options, the levy on the premium rather than on the notional exposure means the headline rate understates the cost relative to the capital at risk on a short-premium position.

Stamp duty is collected centrally in the securities market rather than at state rates, which is a different position from stamp duty on immovable property, where the rate is set by the state and is a substantial transaction cost.
These levies are small in percentage terms but are incurred on both legs, and their cumulative effect over a high-turnover strategy is materially larger than their per-transaction magnitude suggests.
notes: Marked provisional because the exact rates and rate structures differ by instrument and have been revised over time. Arthanomy teaches the comparison method and requires readers to confirm the current rate card from the exchange before relying on a computed cost.

title: House property income and the 30% standard deduction
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.22 to s.24; under the Income-tax Act, 2025 the house-property provisions are respectively at s.20 to s.22, with the interest deduction at s.22.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Slab rates on the net annual value after the deductions below.
exemptionLimit: For a self-occupied property, the annual value is treated as nil and interest is deductible subject to a monetary ceiling; where the property is let out, the full interest is deductible but the resulting loss set-off against other heads is capped at ₹2,00,000 per year in the old regime, and this set-off is not available in the new regime.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale.
setOffRule: Loss under the house-property head can be set off against other heads only up to ₹2,00,000 in the old regime, and the balance can be carried forward for up to eight assessment years against house-property income. Under the new regime, a loss under this head generally cannot be set off against other heads.
conditions: A flat 30% deduction from the net annual value is available without evidence of actual expenditure, in addition to municipal taxes actually paid.
Property tax actually paid, where borne by the owner, is deductible before applying the 30% deduction.
Unrealised rent and vacancy allowance have specific rules; an owner who genuinely receives no rent for part of the year can claim a vacancy allowance rather than including notional rent.

Interest on borrowed capital is deductible on an accrual basis even where the property is under construction during the construction period, with the pre-construction interest deductible in five equal instalments starting in the year of completion.
The deduction is not available against deemed letting for a second self-occupied property except under the specified conditions, which depend on the regime chosen.
Arthanomy always computes a rental yield net of municipal taxes, maintenance, vacancy and tax because the gross yield is not an investment return.

title: Business income, presumptive taxation and the ₹3 crore / ₹75 lakh thresholds
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.28 to s.44, with presumptive regimes at s.44AD for eligible businesses and s.44ADA for specified professions, and the audit obligation under s.44AB.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Slab rates for an individual or HUF proprietor; the presumptive regimes allow income to be declared at a prescribed percentage of turnover, with the thresholds for those regimes raised where the taxpayer's cash receipts are within the prescribed proportion of total receipts.
exemptionLimit: Not applicable.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale; the enhanced rates apply at high total income.
setOffRule: Business losses may be set off against other heads except salary in the same year and may be carried forward for eight assessment years against business income, provided the business is continued and the return is filed by the due date.
conditions: Presumptive taxation is an election with consequences: declaring income below the presumptive rate in a later year can attract audit and can affect the ability to use the presumptive regime again for five assessment years.

The distinction between a business and an investment is central to Arthanomy's business-ownership articles: buying an equity stake is investing in an asset, while operating a business consumes owner time, working capital and management attention, and the return to each is not comparable.
Book-keeping obligations, advance-tax obligations and audit obligations all scale with turnover, which is a real operating cost of business ownership rather than an administrative footnote.
Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the return-of-income provision formerly at s.139 is at s.263. Business provisions are reorganised and section references must be re-verified for Tax Year 2026-27.
notes: Marked provisional on the current monetary thresholds for the presumptive regimes and audit, which have been amended and which Arthanomy has not individually re-verified for the current year.

title: Capital-gains exemptions on reinvestment: s.54, s.54EC, s.54F and s.54B
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.54 (residential house to residential house), s.54B (agricultural land to agricultural land), s.54D, s.54EC (specified bonds), s.54F (any long-term asset other than a residential house to a residential house) and s.54GB.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable; the timing tests are the reinvestment windows, which differ by section.
taxRate: Exemption from capital-gains tax on the eligible amount; the underlying gain remains taxable to the extent not reinvested or to the extent the conditions are breached.
exemptionLimit: s.54EC is capped at ₹50 lakh of investment in specified bonds across a financial year and the following financial year, with a five-year lock-in. s.54 and s.54F are subject to ownership tests on the number of residential houses owned on the date of transfer, and s.54F produces a proportionate exemption rather than a full one.
surchargeRule: Not applicable to the exempt amount.
cessRule: Not applicable to the exempt amount.
setOffRule: Not applicable to the exempt amount.
conditions: Purchase must be completed within one year before or two years after the transfer, or construction within three years.

If the reinvestment cannot be completed before the return due date, the amount must be deposited in a Capital Gains Accounts Scheme account before the due date; failing to do so forfeits the exemption even if the reinvestment later happens.
For s.54 and s.54F, the residential house must be in India for the exemption to apply (the India condition applies to the s.54 and s.54F reinvestment).
Breach of the lock-in conditions, including transferring the new asset within the specified period, reverses the exemption and revives the original liability with interest.
Where the assessee owns more than the permitted number of residential houses on the date of transfer, s.54 and s.54F relief is not available — a condition that is frequently overlooked.
The exemption is an exemption, not a deferral, only if every condition is met permanently; partial compliance produces partial exemption with interest exposure.
notes: s.54EC bonds carry a lock-in and a below-market coupon relative to the tax saved; the comparison between paying tax and buying the bond is a real calculation and Arthanomy provides it rather than assuming the exemption is always better.

title: Presumptive taxation for specified professions
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.44ADA.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Income is deemed to be a prescribed percentage of gross receipts, subject to the monetary ceiling on gross receipts, with the ceiling raised where the prescribed proportion of receipts is received through digital channels.
exemptionLimit: Not applicable.
surchargeRule: Ordinary scale.
setOffRule: A taxpayer opting for the presumptive regime cannot separately claim deductions under the ordinary provisions for that business, and depreciation is deemed to have been allowed.
conditions: The list of specified professions is a closed list. A taxpayer providing consulting or freelance software services may or may not fall within it depending on the specific profession and the nature of the engagement.

Where income is declared at the presumptive rate, the taxpayer is relieved of maintaining books for that business, but the option is not free: actual expenses above the deemed allowance are simply not deductible.
Advance tax in a single instalment is permitted for a taxpayer covered by the presumptive regime, which is a genuine cash-flow simplification.
The consequence of opting out in a later year includes five years of ineligibility where income was computed under the presumptive provisions.
notes: Marked provisional on the current monetary ceilings, which have been amended and which Arthanomy has not re-verified for the current year.

title: Tax deduction at source on interest other than securities
assetClass: Deposits, P2P lending and other interest
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.194A.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Tax is deducted at the prescribed rate on interest above the applicable monetary threshold, which differs between banks, co-operative banks, post-office schemes, and other payers, and which is higher for a senior citizen.
exemptionLimit: The thresholds below which no deduction is required differ by payer category and have been raised over time.
surchargeRule: Not applicable to the deduction, which is computed at the flat statutory rate rather than at the recipient's marginal rate.
setOffRule: Not applicable; the deducted amount is creditable against the taxpayer's final liability and refundable if excess.
conditions: Tax deducted at source is not a final tax. Because it is deducted at a flat rate rather than at the taxpayer's marginal rate, a taxpayer in the 30% slab will have a shortfall while a taxpayer below the exemption threshold will have paid too much and will need to claim a refund.
Filing a declaration to avoid deduction is appropriate only where the taxpayer's total income is genuinely below the taxable threshold; filing it otherwise creates interest exposure.
Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the tax-deduction provisions are consolidated at s.393 and the interest thresholds have been revised. The section references change for Tax Year 2026-27.
The threshold is a deduction threshold, not an exemption: interest below it remains fully taxable and must be reported.
notes: Marked provisional on current thresholds, which differ by payer category and have been revised repeatedly.

title: Tax audit and books of account obligations
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.44AA and s.44AB.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Not applicable — this rule concerns obligations rather than rates. The cost of an audit is a real professional fee that reduces the net return on a trading or business activity.
exemptionLimit: Specified businesses and professions are exempt from maintaining books, and the audit requirement is subject to monetary thresholds that differ by the nature of the business and by the proportion of digital receipts.
surchargeRule: Not applicable.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: Turnover for derivatives is computed by a specified method that does not equal the aggregate contract value, and the difference determines whether an audit is required.
A taxpayer who declares income below the presumptive rate may be required to have accounts audited irrespective of turnover.
Failing to obtain an audit where required is a default with a monetary penalty, which can exceed the entire trading profit of a small account.
The audit-or-not question is a reason that a small derivatives account should be evaluated on after-cost, after-compliance terms rather than on the gross trading result.
notes: Marked provisional on current thresholds and the turnover-computation method applicable to derivative transactions in the current year.

title: Unlisted equity shares — acquisition, holding and transfer
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.112 for long-term gains, s.56(2)(x) for the receipt of shares below fair market value, and s.2(42A) for the holding-period threshold.
holdingPeriodRule: More than 24 months. Unlisted shares are not s.112A assets, so there is no ₹1,25,000 exemption.
taxRate: 12.5% on long-term gains without indexation; slab rates on short-term gains; slab rates on the excess where shares are received for consideration below fair market value.
exemptionLimit: None for unlisted shares.
surchargeRule: 15% cap for long-term gains under s.112; ordinary scale for short-term gains.
setOffRule: Standard sequencing; short-term losses are more flexible than long-term losses.
conditions: Valuation is governed by the prescribed rule, and a transaction at a price materially different from the prescribed fair market value creates a tax consequence for one or both parties.

Because unlisted shares are not traded on a recognised exchange, there is no objective price at the transaction date; the prescribed valuation method becomes the operative fact. This is a genuine audit risk area.
A sale of unlisted shares may attract tax deduction at source by the buyer in specified circumstances, which changes the practical cash flow.
The absence of a securities transaction tax means s.111A and s.112A do not apply at all — a structural difference from listed equity that materially worsens the rate for a short-term holder.

A company that subsequently lists converts an unlisted holding into a listed holding; the acquisition cost remains the original cost and the holding period continues to run, so a pre-IPO holding can qualify as long-term shortly after listing. The exact treatment should be confirmed for the specific case.
notes: Marked provisional on the valuation-rule mechanics and the withholding obligation, which Arthanomy has not individually verified for the current year.

title: Choosing between the default new regime and the old regime
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961, s.115BAC (new regime, the default); under the Income-tax Act, 2025 the corresponding provision is s.202.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: New regime: nil to ₹4,00,000; 5% to ₹8,00,000; 10% to ₹12,00,000; 15% to ₹16,00,000; 20% to ₹20,00,000; 25% to ₹24,00,000; 30% above ₹24,00,000. Old regime for an individual below 60: nil to ₹2,50,000; 5% to ₹5,00,000; 20% to ₹10,00,000; 30% above ₹10,00,000, with a higher basic exemption for resident senior and super senior citizens.
exemptionLimit: Rebate: ₹60,000 under the new regime where taxable income does not exceed ₹12,00,000, and ₹12,500 under the old regime where taxable income does not exceed ₹5,00,000. The rebate is not available against income chargeable at special rates such as capital gains. A standard deduction of ₹75,000 applies to salary under the new regime and ₹50,000 under the old regime.
surchargeRule: Old regime retains 37% above ₹5 crore; the new regime caps at 25%. The 15% cap on s.111A, s.112, s.112A and dividend income applies in both regimes.
cessRule: Health and education cess at 4% in both regimes.
setOffRule: Set-off of a loss under the house-property head against other heads is available in the old regime up to ₹2,00,000 and is restricted in the new regime. This is one of the structural differences that changes the optimal choice for a mortgaged owner-occupied property.
conditions: The new regime is the default. A taxpayer without business income can switch between regimes in each assessment year; a taxpayer with business income can switch out of the default only once in a lifetime, using the prescribed form, before the return due date.

The new regime disallows most Chapter VI-A deductions, HRA, LTA, and interest on a self-occupied property, but retains the standard deduction, the employer NPS contribution under s.80CCD(2) and the Agniveer contribution deduction.

Because the new regime's slabs are substantially more generous at low and middle income, the old regime is beneficial only where the sum of foregone deductions exceeds the slab advantage. The two must be computed on the actual numbers, not estimated.

Marginal relief applies where income slightly exceeds the ₹12,00,000 rebate threshold under the new regime, so income just above the threshold is not taxed at an effective rate far above the nominal 10%.
The comparison must be run on total income including capital gains, because special-rate income sits alongside slab income and affects the surcharge bands.
Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the new regime remains the default under s.202 and the slabs are unchanged for Tax Year 2026-27.
workedExampleSummary: Taxable income ₹12,00,000 under the new regime: slab tax ₹60,000 regresses to nil after the s.87A rebate. At ₹13,00,000 the slab tax is ₹75,000 and the rebate is no longer available; marginal relief is not applicable at that level because the shortfall mechanism operates only in the narrow band above ₹12,00,000.
notes: Arthanomy's regime-comparison calculator computes both regimes on the user's actual deduction profile rather than asserting that one regime is universally better.

title: Fair market value, valuation rules and the role of a registered valuer
assetClass: Unlisted equity, property and other assets without a market price
provision: Income-tax Act, 1961 — the valuation rules prescribed under the relevant provisions and the registered-valuer framework under the Companies Act and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
holdingPeriodRule: Not applicable.
taxRate: Not applicable.
exemptionLimit: Not applicable.
surchargeRule: Not applicable.
setOffRule: Not applicable.
conditions: The tax system prescribes its own valuation method for many transactions, and the prescribed method is not necessarily the price agreed between the parties or the price a professional valuer would derive in an arm's-length transaction.
A registered valuer's certificate does not control the tax valuation where a prescribed rule applies; it is evidence, not a determination.
For property, stamp-duty value rather than the transaction price can be relevant to the tax computation in specific circumstances.

Where a transaction is not at arm's length between related parties, the tax provisions on inadequate consideration can create a liability for either side, and the disclosure obligations differ by provision.
Arthanomy does not provide valuations, and its due-diligence content is explicitly not a substitute for title verification or a professional valuation.
notes: Marked provisional because the valuation rules are numerous, provision-specific and amended frequently; Arthanomy describes the structure rather than reproducing rules it has not individually verified.
